title: Curiosity Rover Spots Mysterious Cliffs Ahead on Mars
summary:
NASA's Curiosity rover has sent back a beautiful new panorama of Mars that gives scientists their clearest look yet at a line of strange cliffs shaped by wind.

The rover took six photos with its Mastcam camera on August 11, at 8:30 in the morning Mars time. Scientists joined them into one wide view. They chose not to adjust the colors, so the picture keeps the real look of a Martian morning, with bluish tones in front and sunlight on the cliffs in the distance.

These cliffs are called yardangs. They are ridges carved by wind, and they stretch about 10 miles across part of Mount Sharp, a mountain about 3 miles tall. Curiosity has been climbing Mount Sharp since 2014. It recently gained about 0.6 miles in height, a bigger climb than any other rover on Mars.

Mount Sharp is made of many layers of rock, and each layer holds clues about a different time in Mars's past. These layers have shown that billions of years ago there were lakes and streams in this area. When the water dried up, salty minerals were left behind.

But the yardang layer is puzzling. Its color is different from the rocks around it, and its layers tilt at an odd angle. "It almost appears plastered on," said Ashwin Vasavada, a Curiosity scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. He said one idea is that it may be ash from ancient volcanic eruptions.

Over the next year, Curiosity will keep driving through rocks full of minerals that formed as Mars dried out. Scientists hope it reaches the bottom of the cliffs in 2027, where it can study them with its robotic arm and help solve the mystery.
why_it_matters: Each rock layer Curiosity studies helps explain how Mars changed from a world with lakes and streams to the dry planet we see today.

background_read: Curiosity is a car-sized NASA rover exploring Gale Crater on Mars, where it has been climbing Mount Sharp since 2014.
Mount Sharp is built from many rock layers, and each layer works like a page in a history book that records what Mars was like long ago.
By studying these layers, scientists learned that the area once had lakes and streams before Mars became the dry, cold planet it is today.
Rovers carry cameras and tools on robotic arms so scientists on Earth can study rocks up close without traveling to Mars.
